t.4.55.1: All those monkeys had sat down on the mountain plateau to fast unto death, and the king of vultures approached that very place.
t.4.55.2: There was a long-lived bird, Sāmpāti by name, the glorious brother of Jaṭāyus, renowned for his strength and valour.
t.4.55.3: Having come out from a cave of the great mountain Vindhya, he saw the monkeys seated there and, his heart filled with joy, spoke these words.
t.4.55.4: Destiny, it is said, follows a man in this world according to its ordinance, for this food, ordained for me, has come to me after a long time.
t.4.55.5: Having looked at those monkeys, the bird spoke these words: "I shall devour these monkeys one after another, each one as he dies."
t.4.55.6: Having heard those words of the bird greedy for food, Aṅgada, greatly distressed, then spoke to Hanūmān.
t.4.55.7: Look! Under the pretext of Sītā, Yama himself, the son of Vivasvat, has come to this place for the destruction of the vānaras.
t.4.55.8: Rāma's task has not been accomplished, nor has the king's command been carried out; this unforeseen calamity has suddenly come upon the monkeys.
t.4.55.9: The deed that Jaṭāyus, king of vultures, did there out of his wish to serve Vaidehī, all of that you have heard in full.
t.4.55.10: Just as we do, so too all creatures, even those born in animal wombs, do what is dear to Rāma, giving up their lives.
t.4.55.11: For Rāghava's sake we have worn ourselves out, having given up all thought of our lives; we have entered the wild forests, and yet we do not see Maithilī.
t.4.55.12: But that king of vultures is happy, slain by Rāvaṇa in battle; he is freed from the fear of Sugrīva and has gone to the supreme state.
t.4.55.13: Through the death of Jaṭāyus and of King Daśaratha, and through the abduction of Vaidehī, the monkeys have come into grave peril.
t.4.55.14: The dwelling of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in the forest together with Sītā, and likewise the slaying of Vālin by the arrow of Rāghava.
t.4.55.15: Likewise, the slaughter of all the rākṣasas through Rāma's wrath: indeed, all this calamity has been brought about by the granting of boons to Kaikeyī.
t.4.55.16: Then, having heard those words that had come forth from Aṅgada's mouth, the sharp-beaked, loud-voiced vulture spoke these words.
t.4.55.18: How did the battle between the rākṣasa and the vulture take place in Janasthāna? After a long time, today, I have heard this name of my brother.
t.4.55.17: Who is this who, with his voice, proclaims the slaying of Jaṭāyus, my brother dearer to me than my very life, as though making my mind tremble?
t.4.55.19: O bulls among the vānaras, I would like to hear of the destruction of my younger brother, who knew the worth of virtues and was praiseworthy for his feats of valour.
t.4.55.21: Because my wings were scorched by the rays of the sun, I am unable to move about. O subduers of foes, I would like to come down from this mountain.
t.4.55.20: How did Daśaratha become the friend of my brother Jaṭāyus, who dwelt in Janasthāna, that very brother of mine? Daśaratha, whose dear eldest son is Rāma, beloved of his elders?
